titulo: An ageing continent: can pension systems survive?

fuente.nota: Written for the language panel. The figures are approximate and should not be cited as a source.

parrafos: In many small towns in rural Europe, the primary school has closed its doors and the building now houses a day centre for the elderly. Similar stories can be told from inland Spain to eastern Germany. The continent is growing older faster than almost any other region of the world, and nowhere is the strain more visible than in the systems that pay for retirement.

The demographic arithmetic is stark. Fertility rates across the European Union hover around 1.5 children per woman, well below the replacement level of roughly 2.1. At the same time, life expectancy has risen by several years over recent decades, interrupted only briefly by the pandemic. The large cohorts born during the baby boom of the 1950s and 1960s are now leaving the labour market en masse. As a result, the old-age dependency ratio, which compares people over 65 with those of working age, is set to rise sharply: where there are today roughly three people of working age for every person over 65, by mid-century there may be fewer than two.

Most European pension systems were designed for a very different world. They operate largely on a pay-as-you-go basis, meaning that today's contributions from workers and employers finance today's pensions, rather than being saved and invested. The model works admirably when the population pyramid is wide at the base and narrow at the top. It becomes far more fragile when the pyramid turns into something closer to a column, or even an inverted triangle, because fewer contributors must support more beneficiaries for longer periods.

Governments have not stood idle. Over the past three decades, almost every member state has reformed its system at least once, and often several times. The most common lever has been the retirement age, which has been raised, or linked automatically to life expectancy, in countries ranging from Denmark to Italy. Others have tightened the rules for early retirement, lengthened the number of years used to calculate benefits or changed the way pensions are updated each year. Sweden pioneered a system of notional accounts, in which each worker's entitlements depend on the contributions he or she has made and on the expected length of retirement.

These reforms have had a measurable effect. Projections by European institutions suggest that, despite the ageing of the population, public spending on pensions as a share of GDP will rise only moderately in many countries over the coming decades, and may even fall in some. The reason is that the reforms have reduced the generosity of future pensions relative to wages. In other words, part of the burden has been shifted quietly from today's taxpayers to tomorrow's retirees, who can expect replacement rates noticeably lower than those enjoyed by their parents.

That trade-off is politically explosive. In France, attempts to raise the minimum retirement age have repeatedly brought hundreds of thousands of people onto the streets, and the most recent reform, pushed through in 2023 without a final parliamentary vote, has remained under pressure ever since. Elsewhere, governments have backtracked, reintroducing full indexation to inflation or suspending automatic mechanisms as soon as they began to bite. Older voters, who turn out at elections in greater numbers than the young, form a powerful constituency that few politicians dare to antagonise.

Spain offers an instructive example. After a reform in 2013 that linked pension increases to the financial health of the system and introduced a sustainability factor, the backlash from pensioners was so strong that the measures were first frozen and then repealed. The reforms adopted since 2021 have taken the opposite approach, restoring the link with consumer prices and seeking to close the gap mainly by raising revenue, notably through higher contributions on top salaries and an intergenerational equity mechanism. Supporters see a fairer balance between generations; sceptics, including some independent fiscal watchdogs, doubt that the extra income will be enough to cover the rising bill.

Raising revenue is indeed the other side of the equation, and here the labour market holds the key. The ratio that really matters for the finances of a pay-as-you-go system is not the number of older people relative to the working-age population, but the number of pensioners relative to people actually in work. Increasing the employment rate of women, young people and older workers can therefore offset a significant part of the demographic shock. Countries such as the Netherlands and the Nordic states, where participation remains high well into people's sixties, are in a far more comfortable position than those where many workers leave the labour market early.

Immigration is the most controversial lever. Younger migrants who find formal employment pay contributions and taxes and can ease the pressure on public budgets in the short and medium term. Yet economists caution that migrants also grow old and acquire pension rights of their own, so immigration postpones the problem rather than solving it, unless inflows remain high indefinitely. Its success also depends on how well newcomers are integrated: migrants stuck in informal or low-paid jobs contribute far less than their numbers might suggest. And in many countries public opinion sets clear limits on what governments can propose.

A further option is to rely more on funded savings. Occupational schemes and individual pension accounts, in which contributions are invested in financial markets, already play a large role in countries such as the Netherlands, Denmark and the United Kingdom. Advocates argue that they diversify risk and help to deepen European capital markets, which could in turn finance investment and growth. Critics reply that funded pensions are exposed to market volatility and inflation, carry management costs and tend to benefit higher earners, who find it easier to save. Moreover, moving from one system to another imposes a double burden on the transition generation, which must pay for current pensions while saving for its own.

Productivity, finally, may be the least discussed but most decisive variable. If each worker produces more, a smaller workforce can still sustain a growing number of retirees without a fall in living standards. Automation and artificial intelligence could, in principle, compensate for labour shortages, although the evidence so far is mixed and the gains are unevenly distributed. Investment in education, lifelong learning and healthier ageing would also allow people to work longer in jobs that suit them, rather than simply forcing them to stay at their posts.

So can Europe's pension systems survive? The honest answer is that they will, but probably not in their current form. The coming decades are likely to bring a combination of later retirement, slower growth in benefits, higher contributions and a larger role for private savings. The real question is how the adjustment is shared between generations and social groups, and whether it is planned openly or imposed abruptly by events. A system that young people no longer believe in is, in the end, as fragile as one that runs out of money.
titulo_es: An ageing continent: can pension systems survive?
resumen_es: An analysis of how the ageing of Europe's population puts pressure on pay-as-you-go pension systems and of the options for sustaining them: parametric reforms, more revenue and employment, immigration, funded savings and productivity.

ideas_clave.idea: Europe is ageing rapidly because of low fertility, longer lives and the retirement of the baby boomers, so the number of workers per older person is set to fall markedly.
Pay-as-you-go systems, in which current contributions fund current pensions, become vulnerable when contributors shrink relative to beneficiaries.
Repeated reforms, especially later retirement ages and less generous benefit formulas, have contained projected spending, but at the cost of lower future replacement rates.
Such reforms provoke strong political resistance, as shown by protests in France and by Spain, which reversed its 2013 reform and now relies mainly on higher revenue.
Higher employment among women, young and older people can offset much of the demographic shock, since what counts is the ratio of pensioners to people in work.
Immigration can provide temporary relief but does not solve the problem permanently and depends on integration and public acceptance.
Funded pension savings could diversify risk and develop capital markets, though they bring volatility, costs, inequality and a transition burden.
Productivity growth, supported by technology, education and healthier ageing, is perhaps the decisive factor.
Pension systems will probably survive in a modified form; the key issue is how fairly and transparently the adjustment is shared, as young people's trust is essential.

resumen_modelo: The article analyses whether Europe's pension systems can withstand demographic ageing. With fertility well below replacement level, rising life expectancy and the baby-boom generation retiring, the ratio of working-age people to those over 65 is expected to drop from about three to fewer than two by mid-century. This poses a serious threat to pay-as-you-go schemes, which use current contributions to pay current pensions. Most countries have already reformed their systems, chiefly by raising or indexing the retirement age and tightening benefit rules, which has kept projected spending under control but will make future pensions less generous relative to wages. Nevertheless, such measures meet fierce opposition, as illustrated by protests in France and by Spain's decision to abandon its 2013 reform in favour of inflation indexation and additional revenue, a strategy whose sufficiency is questioned. The author then reviews other levers. Raising employment rates is crucial, since the real constraint is the number of pensioners per worker. Immigration may help in the short term but merely delays the problem and depends on successful integration. Greater reliance on funded savings could diversify risk, yet it entails market exposure, costs, inequality and a double burden during the transition. Ultimately, productivity may be decisive. The article concludes that pension systems will endure only in a changed form, and that the fairness and transparency of the adjustment will determine whether younger generations continue to trust them.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: The fertility rate in the EU is slightly above the replacement level.
preguntas.cita: hover around 1.5 children per woman, well below the replacement level of roughly 2.1
preguntas.explicacion: The fertility rate is around 1.5 children per woman, well below the replacement level (2.1), not slightly above it.

preguntas.enunciado: Choose the correct option according to the text.
preguntas.pregunta: According to the article, how many people of working age might there be for each person over 65 by mid-century?
preguntas.cita: by mid-century there may be fewer than two
preguntas.explicacion: Today there are about three people of working age for every person over 65, and by the middle of the century there could be fewer than two. “About three” is the current figure, not the future one.

preguntas.enunciado: Find the expression in paragraph 3 for a pension system in which current contributions pay current pensions (es: sistema de reparto).
preguntas.pregunta: Find the expression for a system in which current contributions pay current pensions.
preguntas.cita: They operate largely on a pay-as-you-go basis
preguntas.explicacion: “Pay-as-you-go” is the technical English term for this system, as opposed to “funded” (es: capitalización).

preguntas.enunciado: Choose the correct option according to the text.
preguntas.pregunta: What has been the most common instrument of pension reform in Europe?
opciones: Raising or indexing the retirement age
respuestas: Raising or indexing the retirement age
preguntas.cita: The most common lever has been the retirement age, which has been raised, or linked automatically to life expectancy
preguntas.explicacion: The text identifies the retirement age as the most common lever. Notional accounts are the Swedish case, higher contributions on high salaries are the Spanish case, and privatisation is not mentioned.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: Thanks to past reforms, future retirees can expect pensions that are lower in relation to wages than those of their parents.
preguntas.cita: who can expect replacement rates noticeably lower than those enjoyed by their parents
preguntas.explicacion: The text explains that reforms have reduced the generosity of future pensions relative to wages, so replacement rates will be lower.

preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning “reversed their position”.
preguntas.explicacion: “To backtrack” means to retract or go back on a decision or policy.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.

preguntas.explicacion: The text says explicitly that the reform was passed without a final parliamentary vote.

preguntas.enunciado: Choose the correct option according to the text.
preguntas.pregunta: How have Spain's reforms since 2021 differed from the 2013 reform?
opciones: They raised the retirement age to 70
They restored indexation to prices and focused on raising revenue
They introduced a stronger sustainability factor
They replaced public pensions with individual accounts
respuestas: They restored indexation to prices and focused on raising revenue
preguntas.cita: restoring the link with consumer prices and seeking to close the gap mainly by raising revenue
preguntas.explicacion: The reforms since 2021 restore CPI indexation of pensions and seek more revenue. The sustainability factor belonged to the 2013 reform and was repealed; retirement at 70 and individual accounts are not mentioned.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: Spain's intergenerational equity mechanism will end in 2050.
preguntas.explicacion: The text mentions the intergenerational equity mechanism, but says nothing about how long it will last or when it will end.

preguntas.enunciado: Answer in your own words (1–3 sentences).
preguntas.pregunta: Why does the author claim that the labour market “holds the key”?
respuestas: Because the finances of a pay-as-you-go system depend on the number of pensioners per person actually working, not per person of working age. Raising employment among women, young and older people therefore increases contributors and offsets much of the ageing effect.
preguntas.cita: the number of pensioners relative to people actually in work
preguntas.explicacion: The key is to distinguish between the working-age population and the employed population: more employment means more contributors and offsets part of the demographic shock.

preguntas.enunciado: Choose the correct option according to the text.
preguntas.pregunta: Why do economists say immigration only postpones the pension problem?
opciones: Because migrants also age and earn pension rights
Because migrants usually return home before retiring
Because the EU limits labour migration
respuestas: Because migrants also age and earn pension rights
preguntas.cita: migrants also grow old and acquire pension rights of their own
preguntas.explicacion: Immigrants also grow old and acquire pension rights. The text says that they do pay contributions if they have formal jobs, and it does not mention return migration or EU limits.

preguntas.enunciado: Find a word in paragraph 10 that means “supporters, defenders”.
preguntas.cita: Advocates argue that they diversify risk
preguntas.explicacion: “Advocates” are the supporters or defenders of an idea; here it is contrasted with “Critics”.

preguntas.enunciado: Answer in your own words (1–3 sentences).
preguntas.pregunta: What is the “double burden” mentioned in connection with funded pensions?
respuestas: When a country moves from pay-as-you-go to funded pensions, the generation in transition has to finance the pensions of current retirees while also saving for its own retirement.
preguntas.cita: imposes a double burden on the transition generation, which must pay for current pensions while saving for its own
preguntas.explicacion: This is the transition cost: one generation pays twice, for current pensions and for its own savings.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: The article states that artificial intelligence has already solved labour shortages in Europe.
preguntas.cita: although the evidence so far is mixed and the gains are unevenly distributed
preguntas.explicacion: The text says that automation and AI could in principle offset labour shortages, but that the evidence so far is mixed.

preguntas.enunciado: Answer in your own words (1–3 sentences).
preguntas.pregunta: What does the author mean by the final sentence of the article?
respuestas: That a pension system depends not only on its finances but also on the confidence of the young: if they stop believing they will receive a pension, political support for the system collapses, which makes it just as vulnerable as running out of money.
preguntas.cita: A system that young people no longer believe in is, in the end, as fragile as one that runs out of money
preguntas.explicacion: This is an inference question: intergenerational legitimacy is as important as financial solvency.
